# INTU (Intuit Inc.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand at the business-model level: Intuit sells subscription software to consumers (TurboTax, Credit Karma) and small businesses (QuickBooks, Mailchimp) for tax prep, bookkeeping, payments, payroll, and marketing. No exotic financial engineering, no black-box technology risk in the traditional sense. The one genuine competence-stretching question is whether generative AI hollows out the manual-labor-adjacent value of DIY tax prep and basic bookkeeping — both squarely Intuit's bread and butter — over the next decade. That's a live, unsettled debate, and it's the reason this stock is down over half in twelve months.

## Moat & Durability — Score 6/10
Switching costs are real: QuickBooks is deeply embedded in SMB financial workflows and cross-sold into payroll, payments, and Mailchimp marketing, creating a sticky ecosystem. TurboTax carries a dominant consumer brand in DIY tax filing, and Credit Karma anchors a large consumer financial-data distribution flywheel. Current profitability confirms pricing power is intact today: 80.8% gross margin, 47.0% operating margin. But the moat is not what the market believed it was a year ago — generative AI is a credible, direct threat to the two specific products (DIY tax prep, basic bookkeeping) that make up Intuit's core, and the market has already re-rated the stock hard (-52.4% trailing 12-month return, still -26.2% below the 200-day moving average despite a recent bounce) to reflect that fear. This is a moat under genuine, not hypothetical, pressure, which is why it scores 6 rather than 8-9.

## Management & Capital Allocation
The numbers imply competent stewardship: 22.5% ROE achieved with moderate leverage (debt/equity ~33%, not purely leverage-juiced), and a 5.8% free-cash-flow yield suggests real cash generation. What this packet cannot show: actual integration success of past acquisitions (Credit Karma-, Mailchimp-scale deals), buyback pace, dividend trajectory, or insider ownership/alignment. The most notable oddity in the data is the gap between trailing P/E (20.2x) and forward P/E (12.1x) — implying roughly 67% forward EPS growth against only 10.4% revenue growth. That combination (flattish top-line, huge implied bottom-line inflection) usually means either a one-time charge depressed trailing GAAP earnings and forward estimates reflect a cleaner run-rate, or the Street's forward numbers are simply too optimistic. This packet gives no way to tell which, and 'trustworthy management' here is a reasonable inference from the operating ratios, not a verified fact.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 10.4% and consistently high margins look steady in isolation, but the unexplained 52.4% one-year price collapse and the trailing/forward P/E gap show the market itself is unsure whether this is a normalizing earnings dip or a structural re-rating driven by AI disruption fears. The packet's thesis field is null — no qualitative context available — and momentum shows real turbulence: -20.5% over six months, -52.4% over twelve months, then a sharp +17.7% one-month bounce with RSI at 73.9 (overbought) while price is still well below its 200-day average. That is a market actively re-pricing the story, not a steady compounder trading in a tight band. This fails Munger's 'easy decision' test.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **AI disintermediates the core products directly**: generative AI commoditizes DIY tax prep and basic bookkeeping — not adjacent services, but Intuit's two flagship products — faster than Intuit's own AI investment (Intuit Assist, etc.) can defend share and pricing power.
2. **The forward-earnings inflection doesn't happen**: the implied ~67% jump from trailing to forward EPS reflects either an unresolved one-time hit to trailing earnings or overly optimistic consensus; if actual results land closer to the trailing run-rate, the stock re-rates lower from a price that has already bounced +17.7% in a month on an overbought RSI of 73.9.
3. **Balance-sheet and integration strain**: debt equal to roughly a third of equity, layered on past sizeable acquisitions, becomes a liability if SMB credit conditions or ad-spend (Mailchimp) weaken in a downturn, compounding pressure on a name already showing 5.1% short interest and a near-neutral-to-put-leaning options book (P/C OI ~1.06).

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($90.33B), trailing P/E (20.16x), forward P/E (12.07x), and FCF yield (5.79%) but not share count or share price directly. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~280M diluted share count (a modeling assumption consistent with Intuit's known scale, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $322.6, trailing EPS near $16.00, forward EPS near $26.73, and FCF/share near $18.69. Haircutting FCF for stock-based comp (a real, non-cash-but-real economic cost typical of high-margin SaaS names) to approximate owner earnings gives roughly $16.50/share in normalized owner earnings — deliberately not crediting the full forward-EPS jump, since a 67% one-year earnings inflection on 10.4% revenue growth is exactly the kind of story Munger would want proven, not assumed.

Applying a multiple range to normalized owner earnings:
- **Low case** (conservative: AI-disruption discount applied, no credit for the forward-earnings jump): ~11x owner earnings → ~$180/share.
- **High case** (AI fears prove overstated, forward growth partially validated, multiple approaches what a quality compounder with this margin structure has historically commanded): ~17x owner earnings → ~$280/share.

Midpoint ~$230/share vs. an implied current price of ~$323/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-28.7%** — the stock appears to be pricing in the optimistic (forward-EPS-jump) scenario already, even after a 52% collapse. That is the classic 'cheap for a stated reason, but is it cheap enough' setup: real quality, real risk, and a price that has already partly recovered without the earnings question being resolved.

## The Cloning Caveat
Yacktman Asset Management is the standout signal here: a 0.04%-of-portfolio starter position opened in Q1 2026 was scaled up 6561% by Q2 2026 to 1.57% of portfolio — a deliberate, staged build from a shop with real value-investing pedigree, not a token position. Arnold Van Den Berg (Century Management) opened a new 0.68% position in Q1 2026, and Hillman Capital a new 0.29% stake the same quarter. David Katz (Matrix Asset Advisors) nearly tripled a small position to just 0.15% of portfolio. None of these is a max-conviction, 20-40%-of-fund bet — the largest is under 2% — so this is basket-level corroboration from several value-minded managers converging on a beaten-down quality name, not a statement of overwhelming conviction. The Yacktman scaling pattern is the most informative data point (building conviction over two quarters), but it still argues for 'worth watching closely,' not 'blindly follow.'

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 5/10.** Intuit remains an understandable, historically well-run business with real switching costs and strong current profitability (80.8% gross margin, 47.0% operating margin, 22.5% ROE). But the moat faces its first genuine AI-disruption threat aimed squarely at its two core products, predictability is impaired by an unexplained 52% collapse and an unresolved trailing/forward earnings gap, and on a normalized-owner-earnings basis the current price does not look cheap enough to compensate for that uncertainty — the recent 17.7% bounce (RSI 73.9, overbought) has already priced in some optimism. Superinvestor buying, led by Yacktman's staged build, corroborates that this is worth serious attention, but it is not yet a substitute for a better price or more clarity on the earnings normalization story.
momentum_thesis: INTU is a classic bounce-in-a-downtrend setup: the 1-month +17.7% thrust looks impressive in isolation but sits on top of a stock down 20.5% over six months and 52.4% over twelve, and price remains 26% below its 200DMA — the longer trend hasn't turned, it's a stretched rubber band. RSI14 at 73.9 confirms the short-term move is overbought, raising mean-reversion odds into the next few weeks rather than continuation. Positioning offers little squeeze fuel: short interest is just 5.1% of float with only 2.8 days to cover, so this isn't short-covering panic driving the pop, and put/call OI at 1.06 shows options traders are still mildly hedged rather than chasing calls. The superinvestor activity cuts toward a value read, not a momentum one — Yacktman built a new stake in Q1 and added aggressively (+6561% shares) in Q2, joined by Van Den Berg and Hillman Capital initiating fresh positions, all classic value shops buying into weakness rather than strength, which is contrarian conviction, not confirmation of a trend change. Forward PE of 12x against a trailing 20x implies the Street expects an earnings inflection, but until price reclaims the 200DMA the tape itself hasn't validated that thesis. Treat the 1-month pop as a relief rally inside a still-intact downtrend until it clears the 200DMA on volume.
